plan.topic: Bootleg 'Reta': CBS News (Oct 13) reported that the FDA received two death reports after people took products sold as retatrutide
plan.angle: Answer within 10 s: 'Retatrutide isn't approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. CBS reported two deaths reported to the FDA after people took products claiming to be it. It hasn't been established that the products caused the deaths, and nobody knows what the vials contained.' Credit the details to CBS News and keep its exact wording. Explain that the trial results came from Lilly's drug, made and tested under medical supervision, while products sold online may not match their labels. Cite the FDA's own warning page on unapproved GLP-1 products directly. Never name a seller, show a vial, or mention doses or sourcing. Better route: ask your prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial. Close with the prescriber line. 170 words or fewer.

package.title: Did bootleg 'Reta' cause 2 deaths? What's confirmed #shorts
package.description:
CBS News (Oct 13, 2026) reported two deaths reported to the FDA after people took products sold as retatrutide. CBS says the details aren't verified, and the reports alone don't prove the products caused the deaths. Retatrutide itself is investigational, not FDA-approved as of Oct 2026, and still in clinical trials.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether an approved option is right for you.

Sources:
1. CBS News, "Two deaths were reported to the FDA. Is the bootleg weight-loss drug "Reta" to blame?" (2026) - https://www.cbsnews.com/news/deaths-reported-fda-bootleg-reta-weight-loss-drug/
2. FDA, "FDA's Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss" (current as of Oct 1, 2026) - https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss
3. NEJM, "Triple–Hormone-Receptor Agonist Retatrutide for Obesity — A Phase 2 Trial" (2023) - https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2301972

factcheck.summary: All factual claims match their sources. The CBS News article (Oct 13, 2026) supports each point: 2 deaths were reported to the FDA, the details aren't verified, the reports alone don't prove the drugs caused the deaths, and the FDA declined to say whether it had verified them. It also carries both Lilly statements (the "black-market retatrutide" quote and "too much, too little, or the wrong active ingredient") and says retatrutide is unapproved and generally only available in trials. The FDA page (content current as of 10/01/2026) says word for word that unapproved versions "do not undergo FDA's review for safety, effectiveness and quality before they are marketed". It also says retatrutide has "not been found safe and effective for any condition". The NEJM 2023 Phase 2 trial exists at the cited URL. Framing is careful: claims stay with the right source, causation is explicitly not claimed, nobody is told where to buy, and the piece ends with the prescriber line. Two minor fixes: one attribution label and one optional strengthening with FDA wording.

issues.problem: The fact card is about the trial data, which comes from the NEJM Phase 2 trial (s3), not from Lilly's statements to CBS. The source tag doesn't say the line it's attached to.
issues.fix: Set attribution to: "Phase 2 trial, NEJM 2023; Lilly via CBS News, Oct 13, 2026"

issues.claim: "It isn't FDA-approved as of October 2026, and it's still being tested in clinical trials."
issues.problem: This is accurate (CBS + FDA). Adding the FDA's own wording would make the status line stronger and attribute it to the agency directly. This is optional.
issues.fix: Optional: "So what's confirmed? Retatrutide is investigational. As of October 2026 it isn't FDA-approved, the FDA says it hasn't been found safe and effective for any condition, and it's still being tested in clinical trials." (Check the word count stays at 170 or fewer.)

audio.soundNotes: Overall music level is already in the target window (-13.5 dB under voice, -15.1 in pauses); nudged gain slightly up (1.05) so pauses breathe a bit more toward -14 dB without pushing the under-speech level past -12. Most SFX sit correctly in the -14 to -20 dB speech range and -6 to -12 in pauses, so the main fix is decluttering: several transition moments stacked 2 identical-sounding layers (swoosh+whoosh or swell+whip at the same timestamp, or duplicate ticks/bubbles within the same beat) pushing a few seconds to 5-6 simultaneous cues — dropped the redundant duplicate in each pair/trio to get back to 2-4 per second. The i28 "bubble" at 19.52s was dangerously loud (-5.7 dB, over the voice) during speech and has been pulled down ~10 dB. Kept the very quiet swell at 27.84s/23.26s as-is since that beat is an intentionally serious, SFX-thin moment. Added five bespoke stings at the story's key beats (cold-open mystery, the FDA-rejection reveal, the trial-vs-black-market contrast, the second reveal, and the warm prescriber closing line) to give the reveals a felt accent without any of them competing with narration.
